articles.title: Brain scans reveal two distinct biological profiles of migraine
articles.summary: A new analysis of brain imaging data suggests that migraines can be categorized into two biological groups based on brain structure and network connectivity, offering a potential new framework for understanding the condition.

articles.title: Brain scans reveal lasting tissue and chemical changes in both long COVID and recovered patients
articles.summary: Brain scans reveal that COVID-19 may leave a lasting physical imprint on the brain. A recent study found altered tissue structure and chemical imbalances in both long COVID patients and those who fully recovered from the virus.

articles.title: Children can understand falsification through evidence as early as age 4
articles.summary: The ability to argue using scientific evidence starts remarkably early. A new German study demonstrates that four-year-olds can effectively use evidence to refute false claims, a critical cognitive skill that expands significantly by age five.

articles.title: A man began hearing voices from his body parts after receiving testosterone injections
articles.summary: A recent case report details how a 45-year-old man developed severe religious delusions and hallucinations after receiving prescribed testosterone injections. His undiagnosed genetic condition may have increased his vulnerability to these rare psychiatric side effects.

articles.title: Brains of teens with depression remain on high alert to social rejection
articles.summary: Teens with depression show unique brain patterns when facing social rejection. A recent brain imaging study reveals that their amygdala fails to adapt to repeated social threats, keeping them on high alert during difficult peer interactions.

articles.title: Scientists tracked kids for 8 years — the screen time result was unexpected
articles.summary: An eight-year Finnish study found that children who spent more time on screens tended to show better cognitive processing as teenagers, challenging common assumptions about screen use. Researchers say the key may be balancing physical activity with screen activities that encourage learning, creativity, and active thinking.

articles.title: A little-known protein may be fueling Alzheimer’s — and scientists found a way to block it
articles.summary: An experimental Alzheimer’s compound prevented damaging protein clumps from forming in the brains of mice, helping nerve cells survive longer and reducing amyloid buildup. The treatment also appeared to improve heart health and slow some signs of aging, raising hopes for an entirely new way to combat dementia.

articles.title: A stress hormone may help the brain repair itself
articles.summary: A surprising stress-related signal may help the brain repair itself after injury. Researchers found that myelin-producing precursor cells rapidly release the stress hormone CRH near damaged brain tissue, helping control how those cells mature and rebuild protective nerve insulation. The same system also influences brain development and the thickness of myelin later in life. The findings could offer new clues about how early-life stress contributes to psychiatric disorders.

articles.title: A little movement in midlife could pay off for your brain years later
articles.summary: Exercise and healthy blood sugar levels in midlife may help slow cognitive decline decades later. Physical activity appeared especially beneficial for Mexican American adults, suggesting that some brain-protective factors may differ across populations.
